units.name: command-core
units.role: Model the tree of commands a CLI program offers, and run the lifecycle of finding and executing the right one.
units.description: This is the control center of a command-line program built with Cobra. It keeps track of every command and sub-command the program offers, figures out which one the user is asking for based on what they typed, runs the checks and setup that must happen before the command's own logic runs, then runs it and cleans up afterward. It also knows how to print a helpful summary of a command's flags and usage when the user asks for help or gets something wrong. On Windows, it additionally detects if someone double-clicked the program in File Explorer instead of running it from a terminal and shows a short explanation instead of a confusing flash of a window.

effects.description: CheckErr (cobra.go) and the Windows mousetrap warning path (command_win.go) call os.Exit(1) to terminate the process.
command_win.go calls time.Sleep(MousetrapDisplayDuration) to hold the Windows 'run me from a terminal' warning on screen.

Execute()/ExecuteC() default to os.Args[1:] as the command line when SetArgs wasn't called, and getIn/getOut/getErr default to os.Stdin/os.Stdout/os.Stderr; command_win.go also calls fmt.Scanln() to block for a keypress and checks mousetrap.StartedByExplorer() (inspects the parent process).

units.name: args-validators
units.role: Offer ready-made rules for how many/which positional (non-flag) arguments a command accepts.
units.description: This is a small library of ready-made rules for checking the extra words a user types after a command on the command line (called 'positional arguments'). For example, one rule says 'no extra words allowed', another says 'must have at least 2 extra words', another says 'must have between 2 and 5'. A command-line tool built with Cobra picks one of these rules and attaches it to a command; when someone runs the command, this code checks whether what they typed follows the rule and produces a friendly error message if not.

entrypoints.name: PositionalArgs
entrypoints.plain: The shape every argument rule must have: given a command and its leftover arguments, return an error or nil.

entrypoints.name: legacyArgs
entrypoints.plain: The rule used when a command author didn't pick one: root commands with sub-commands reject unknown sub-commands, everything else accepts anything.

entrypoints.name: NoArgs
entrypoints.plain: Reject the command if any extra words were typed.

entrypoints.name: OnlyValidArgs
entrypoints.plain: Reject any extra word that isn't in the command's declared list of valid values.

entrypoints.name: NoDuplicateArgs
entrypoints.plain: Reject the command if the same extra word appears twice.

entrypoints.name: ArbitraryArgs
entrypoints.plain: Accept any extra words, no restriction.

entrypoints.name: MinimumNArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require at least N extra words.

entrypoints.name: MaximumNArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require at most N extra words.

entrypoints.name: ExactArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require exactly N extra words.

entrypoints.name: RangeArgs
entrypoints.plain: Require between min and max extra words.

entrypoints.name: MatchAll
entrypoints.plain: Combine several rules; all must pass.

entrypoints.name: ExactValidArgs
entrypoints.plain: Deprecated shortcut combining ExactArgs and OnlyValidArgs.

units.name: flag-groups
units.role: Let a command declare that some of its flags must be used together, or that exactly one of a set is required, or that a set is mutually exclusive.
units.description: This part of Cobra lets a command's author declare rules about how command-line flags relate to each other: which flags must always be used together, which group needs at least one flag chosen, and which flags cannot be used at the same time. It stores these rules as hidden tags on the flags themselves, then checks them right before a command runs and reports a clear error if the rules are broken. It also has a helper that nudges the shell's tab-completion to suggest the right flags based on these same rules.

units.name: completion-engine
units.role: Decide, at the moment a user presses Tab, what a command, sub-command, or flag should suggest next.
units.description: This is the brain behind Cobra's tab-completion feature. When a user presses Tab in their shell after typing a partial command, the shell script (generated elsewhere) secretly re-runs the program with a hidden '__complete' command. This unit is what answers that hidden call: it figures out what command, subcommand, flag, or flag value the user is in the middle of typing, runs any custom suggestion logic the program author registered, and prints back the list of suggestions plus a directive telling the shell how to display them (for example, don't add a trailing space, or treat results as filenames). It also implements 'ActiveHelp', a mechanism for injecting short contextual hint messages into the suggestion list, and a small debug-logging helper for troubleshooting completion behavior.

units.name: shell-completion-scripts
units.role: Render and (optionally) save the static, shell-specific completion scripts that call back into the program via the completion engine.
units.description: This part of Cobra writes the actual scripts that let users press Tab to auto-complete commands and flags in their terminal. For each supported shell (Bash v1, Bash v2, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell) it builds a large block of shell-script text that knows how to call back into the compiled program to ask 'what comes next?', and it can either hand that text to a caller or save it straight to a file on disk, for example so it can be installed into a system's completion directory. It also provides small helper functions command authors use to tag a flag as 'this expects a filename', 'this expects a directory', 'this is required', or 'this uses a custom completion function' — tags the generated scripts and the completion engine read to decide how to complete that flag.

units.name: doc-generators
units.role: Walk a Command tree and render it as reference documentation in man, Markdown, reStructuredText, or YAML form.
units.description: This is the documentation-generator for programs built with Cobra. Given the tree of commands and sub-commands that make up a CLI application, it walks that tree and writes out human- and machine-readable reference documentation describing each command, its usage, flags, and examples, in four different formats: Unix man pages, Markdown, reStructuredText, and YAML. Callers can either get the generated text handed back in memory or ask the library to write a whole directory of files, one per command, mirroring the command hierarchy.

violations_observed.note: legacyArgs and OnlyValidArgs call the unexported (*Command).findSuggestions method directly instead of going through a published command-core entrypoint; same-package visibility allows it, but findSuggestions is not part of command-core's declared contract.
OnlyValidArgs calls the unexported stringInSlice helper defined in cobra.go rather than a published entrypoint.
MarkFlagsRequiredTogether, MarkFlagsOneRequired, and MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive each call the unexported (*Command).mergePersistentFlags instead of a published entrypoint.

The completion algorithm reaches into several unexported command-core symbols (the isFlagArg helper, the helpFlagName/helpCommandName constants, and the completionCommandGroupID field) rather than a published API; these are scattered, ad-hoc internal reaches rather than a single clear hook.
The bash script generators read the unexported Command.helpCommand field directly instead of a published entrypoint.

getFlagNameCompletions calls the unexported nonCompletableFlag function defined in bash_completions.go; kept as a listed (if unexported) entrypoint of shell-completion-scripts because it is the sole, well-defined hook for this purpose, but it does mean the two units cannot be split into separate packages without exporting it.

violations_observed.location: completions.go / bash_completions.go / zsh_completions.go / fish_completions.go / powershell_completions.go / bash_completionsV2.go
violations_observed.note: completion-engine and shell-completion-scripts depend on each other's entrypoints (completion-engine uses shell-completion-scripts' BashComp* annotation constants and nonCompletableFlag; shell-completion-scripts uses completion-engine's ShellCompRequestCmd/ShellCompDirective* constants and ActiveHelp marker/env-var helpers), forming a two-way coupling rather than a one-directional dependency. Both units are needed together for shell completion to work end-to-end; they were kept separate here because their responsibilities are distinct (deciding *what* to suggest vs. rendering *how* a given shell asks for and displays suggestions), but a stricter layering would require breaking this cycle.

command-core's own execution path has a hard compile-time dependency on unexported symbols in args.go, flag_groups.go, and completions.go; the four units cannot be split into separate Go packages without exporting these call points, even though they are logically distinct concerns.
